doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

title: Why he kept the bass left-handed
summary: Between-set gigs with Billy Taylor's trio made restringing impractical, so he plays a right-handed bass upside down.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Did you think about re-stringing the bass?

I did. I tried that for a while. But then I said, I was playing with Billy Taylor’s trio at the time. And I remember one Saturday in New York, it was like New Year’s Eve every night. The streets were crowded, the cars were bumper to bumper and you couldn’t get anywhere. And I remember us having to go — in between sets — we’d have to go into a studio and say for instance do a quick television thing and go back to the club.

In between sets, yes. And so in those days it was very difficult to get around. So I says I’m not going to have to wait for another cab or something like that, I wanted to just get in the cab with the trio and go over and play whatever bass is there. But if I have to have a special bass, I’m really defeating my whole thing. So I said I’ll play a right handed bass left handed. So that’s what I decided.
That’s interesting that such a — it becomes a practical decision you know, to make this gig and do what I have to do, I can’t afford to change the strings on my bass.
Right. And you don’t have time to go in there and rearrange everything. It would be terrible.
